record.original_question: Extend Chaitin complexity from finite strings to infinite strings, either by using non-terminating programs that generate infinite strings over infinite time or by using computational models that process infinite strings in finite time, such as cellular automata or functions on the reals.

evidence.quote: 9. Chaitin complexity has been defined for finite strings. It would be interesting to extend it to infinite strings. Two ways can be envisaged: (a) using non-terminating programs ... generating infinite strings in an infinite amount of time; (b) using computational models dealing with infinite strings in finite amounts of time (cellular automata, functions on reals, etc.). (F. Geurts)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. Fix a universal prefix-free Turing machine $U$. For a finite binary string $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, the Chaitin (prefix-free Kolmogorov) complexity is
$$H(x) \;=\; \min\{\,|p| : p \in \{0,1\}^*,\; U(p) = x\,\},$$
i.e. the length of a shortest self-delimiting program that, when run on $U$, halts and outputs $x$.

Problem. Define and study a notion of Chaitin complexity for infinite binary strings $\xi \in \{0,1\}^\omega$ that genuinely measures the descriptive size of $\xi$ as a single infinite object (rather than only via the complexities $H(\xi\!\restriction\! n)$ of its finite prefixes). Two natural frameworks should be considered:

(a) Non-terminating computation. Allow programs $p \in \{0,1\}^*$ that, when executed on a universal machine $U^\omega$ designed to output an infinite stream, never halt but produce an infinite output sequence $U^\omega(p) \in \{0,1\}^\omega$ in the limit. Define
$$H^\omega(\xi) \;=\; \inf\{\,|p| : U^\omega(p) = \xi\,\}$$
(with $H^\omega(\xi) = \infty$ if no such program exists), and develop a theory of $H^\omega$ analogous to the theory of $H$.

(b) Infinite computation in finite time. Use computational models that take an infinite string as input and/or produce one as output in a finite amount of "external" time — for example, cellular automata acting on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{Z}}$, computable functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ in the BSS or computable-analysis sense, or other supertask/transfinite computation models — and use them to define a complexity measure on $\{0,1\}^\omega$.

In each framework, give a precise definition, prove its basic invariance (universality up to additive constants), establish the analogues of the standard properties of $H$ (e.g. counting bounds, symmetry of information, relation to algorithmic randomness), and clarify the relationship between the resulting complexity of $\xi$ and the asymptotic behaviour of $H(\xi\!\restriction\! n)$.
artifact.status_search_result: Several partial extensions of Kolmogorov–Chaitin complexity to infinite sequences exist (e.g. via prefix complexities of initial segments and the theory of Martin-Löf random sequences, and via models such as infinite-time Turing machines, BSS machines, and cellular automata), but no single canonical "Chaitin complexity for infinite strings" satisfying all desired properties has been singled out, and the open-ended programmatic question of systematically extending Chaitin complexity in either of the two suggested ways remains a research direction rather than a settled result.

status_evidence.title: Kolmogorov complexity - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The definition can be extended to define a notion of randomness for infinite sequences ... an infinite sequence is random if the prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity of its initial segments grows quickly enough.
status_evidence.claim: Standard extension to infinite sequences proceeds via complexities of finite prefixes, not via a single complexity value for the infinite string itself.

status_evidence.title: Algorithmic information theory - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Algorithmic information theory principally studies complexity measures on strings (or other data structures).
status_evidence.claim: AIT remains an active area; alternative complexity notions for infinite objects continue to be developed.
